teaser.text: Palantir Technologies sells software for organizations whose data is scattered but whose decisions matter. A dollar comes in when an institution buys access and help, then goes out through delivery, engineering, sales and the rest of the company before any profit remains.

blocks.heading: Where could Palantir’s shares be by 2029?

paragraphs.text: At US$199.86 per share, Palantir’s trailing P/E is 170.8×. The probability-weighted forecast reaches US$184.23 per share in October 2029, an 8% loss from today, hinging on cash-flow growth outrunning multiple compression and dilution.

The scenario range runs from US$52.55 in the bear case to US$429.84 in the bull case. The base case is US$177.69 with 60% probability. Durable Bootcamp conversion, broader production adoption and reusable deployments support the upside; slower growth and rising cloud or delivery costs support the downside.

blocks.heading: What has to go right, and what could go wrong for Palantir?

paragraphs.text: The base case grows cash flow to $4,760M in 2027 and then slows as the business scales. It reaches $7,140M in 2029. The reason is continued paid AIP adoption, strong margins and reusable deployments, supported by 84.7% gross margin in the latest quarter. The bear case falls to $2,550M first, as conversion and hosting costs disappoint, then recovers gradually. The bull case reaches $5,440M first and $10,290M by 2029 as Bootcamps convert and delivery becomes more repeatable. These are forecast assumptions, not guidance.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Palantir really make?

paragraphs.text: Palantir’s adjusted free cash flow was $2,270.436 million because it adds back employer payroll taxes linked to stock compensation. A more conservative sensitivity subtracts stock pay, leaving $1,416.558 million. That is not a formal cash-flow line, but it asks how much cash might remain after considering the economic cost of replacing employee shares.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay today for Palantir?

paragraphs.text: The price-to-earnings ratio, or P/E, says how many dollars investors pay for one dollar of annual accounting profit. A 170.8× P/E means paying roughly $171 for each recent dollar of earnings. Free-cash-flow yield measures the cash generated after capital spending against the price paid. At 0.5%, each $100 invested currently represents about fifty cents of annual free cash flow. That is especially demanding beside a 5.22% government-bond yield.

blocks.heading: What has Palantir guided for the year?

paragraphs.text: The hardest target is American commercial revenue, where sales must more than double. That requires customers to move beyond experimenting with artificial intelligence and pay for broader use in daily operations.

blocks.heading: Has Palantir kept its past promises?

paragraphs.text: Management’s promises also have a mixed record. Karp’s 2021 guidance called for annual revenue growth of at least 30% through 2025, but 2023 growth was 17%. A more specific promise held: management expected profitability in every quarter of 2023, and later results established that run under GAAP.

blocks.heading: What do Palantir's last eight quarters show?

paragraphs.text: Revenue reached $1,935.464 million from $1,003.697 million a year earlier. Operating income reached $912.004 million, and operating margin was 47.1%. Operating income is the stronger first test because it measures the software business before investment income and taxes.

blocks.heading: What should I watch in Palantir's next results?

paragraphs.text: The next quarterly report is the clearest operating checkpoint. An estimated reporting date is November 2, 2026, but Palantir must confirm it. The report will show whether revenue is keeping pace as hiring and product spending increase.
